title: Struck silent (Luke 1:18–25)
hook: he doubts and can't speak for nine months; Elizabeth hides and rejoices

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah in the temple, an old priest alone with the incense, and an angel saying fear not. Your line was your prayer is heard. Did you take out an old hope and look at it again? Day five hundred four.

An angel has just promised Zechariah the son he and Elisabeth prayed for. And what does he say? Not thank you. Not finally. He says, in the King James Bible: "Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife well stricken in years." How can I be sure? It's such a human reply. He and his wife are well stricken in years, and after that long, hope can feel dangerous. It's an old reflex: good news arrives, and the first move is to look for the catch. But this time, the messenger is not amused. He tells Zechariah exactly who he is.

"I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings." Then the sign Zechariah asked for, though not the one he wanted: "thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed." Dumb, in older English, means unable to speak. Outside, the crowd is waiting, wondering why he's taking so long. When he finally comes out, he can't say a word to them. He just makes signs with his hands. Here's a detail worth holding onto: near the very end of Luke's Gospel, Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his friends. Some readers see the Gospel opening with a blessing that couldn't be spoken, and closing with one that finally is. Zechariah goes home in silence. And then Elisabeth conceives. Luke says she hid herself five months, and she says: "Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men." Reproach is her own word for the way people had looked at her. Now, she says, the Lord has looked on her. She doesn't announce it. She keeps it close, like something too precious to show yet. So the house is quiet. A man who can't speak, a woman who won't, and a child growing in the silence. Christians have read Zechariah's silence in more than one way: as a consequence of doubt, and also as a gift, months to listen instead of talk. This week has come a long way: a mother who can't forget, a balm, a scroll in Nazareth, the prophets' voices, Luke's careful letter, an old priest's prayer, and now a quiet house where something is growing.
screen: then, large: `THOU SHALT BE DUMB, AND NOT ABLE TO SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a vow of fewer words today. Settle, and breathe. For these minutes, let the silence be complete. No inner commentary if you can help it. When words start up in your head, notice them, and let them pass like Zechariah's crowd outside the door. Then think about the day ahead. Where do you usually talk too much? Filling silences in meetings, explaining yourself, giving advice nobody asked for, arguing online. Choose one of those places and decide to use fewer words there today. If you pray, you can offer your silence to God as a kind of listening. If you don't, simply rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Struck silent. Zechariah asks for proof and loses his voice until the promise comes true, while Elisabeth quietly carries the child.
Your line: silence can grow things. Today, in the place you chose, say less, listen longer, and see what grows in the gap. Day five hundred four, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Some Christians keep times of silence as a way of waiting, especially in Advent, and some monastic rules, like Saint Benedict's, make silence part of daily life.

fork.setup: you're Zechariah. an angel has just promised you a son in your old age. what do you say?
options: how can I be sure? I'm an old man.
fork.reveal: "whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man." Gabriel gives him a sign: silence, until the promise comes true.

original.note: Greek: being silent. Gabriel's word for what Zechariah will be until the child comes.

trapdoor: what you thought: Zechariah was punished for asking a question.
what it means: his doubt is met with a sign of silence, and in the quiet months, the promise grows in Elisabeth.
what a scholar hears: Zechariah comes out unable to speak to the waiting crowd, and Luke's Gospel ends with Jesus lifting his hands to bless, which some read as the blessing completed.

notes: The index hook says 'Elizabeth'; Luke's KJV text spells 'Elisabeth'. The script uses the KJV spelling.
'Nine months' (index hook) is approximate; he speaks again at John's naming on the eighth day after birth (1:59–64). The script avoids a precise count.
The 'unfinished blessing' reading (1:22 and 24:50–51) is a known interpretation, presented as what 'some readers' see. Confirm.
σιωπῶν (Luke 1:20) is the participle 'being silent'. Confirm form and pronunciation.
Social shame of childlessness in that culture stated with 'often'. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'disappointed for decades' and 'maybe you've felt it' (telling the listener what they feel) rewritten from the text's 'well stricken in years'; 'he's supposed to bless them, the way priests did' cut as unsourced (Luke 1:21–22 says only that he could not speak), and 'the last thing Jesus does' softened to 'near the very end' (Luke 24:51–53 continues); the unsourced social claim about childlessness replaced by Elisabeth's own word 'reproach' (1:25); howItsDone no longer repeats day 503's Advent line and drops 'many monastic communities'.
